sections.text:
They say that the expression “with him” is altogether foreign and unusual, whereas “through him” is very familiar to Scripture and common in the usage of the brotherhood. What shall we answer? Blessed are the ears that have not heard such arguments and the hearts kept unwounded by them.

To you who love Christ I say that the Church knows both usages and rejects neither as destroying the other. When we contemplate the majesty of the nature of the Only-begotten and the excellence of his dignity, we bear witness to his glory with the Father. When we consider the gift of good things granted to us, or our own access and reconciliation to God, we confess that this grace is accomplished for us through him and in him. Thus “with whom” properly belongs to doxology, while “through whom” is especially fitting to thanksgiving.

It is false to say that “with whom” is foreign to devout usage. Those who, from love of good order, have preferred the venerable character of antiquity to novelty and have preserved the tradition of the fathers without adulteration have used this expression in town and countryside alike. It is those who have become tired of what is customary and old, like people chasing new fashions, who embrace innovations.

Therefore what our fathers said, we also say: the glory is common to Father and Son, and so we offer the doxology to the Father with the Son. Yet we do not rely merely on the fact that it was handed down by the fathers, for they themselves followed the mind of Scripture and took their starting points from its testimony. Radiance is conceived together with glory, image with archetype, and the Son always with the Father; neither the sequence of the names, much less the nature of the realities, admits separation.

translator_notes: Basil defends both liturgical formulas: 'with the Son' for common glory and 'through the Son' for the economy of divine gifts.
The appeal to the fathers is explicitly subordinated to Scripture in this chapter.
